fields.question: Why does the Moon follow me?
fields.short_answer: The Moon is so far away that your movement barely changes the direction you see it in. Nearby trees sweep past your view, but the Moon seems to keep pace.
fields.big_idea: Faraway things shift less across your view than nearby things. That difference is called parallax.
fields.try_it: Hold up one finger and walk sideways while looking past it at a distant building. Your finger jumps across the view; the building hardly moves.
fields.try_note: Stand still first, then try it somewhere safely away from roads and stairs.
fields.related_prompt: Show me, step by step, how parallax makes the Moon look like it follows us.

fields.question: Why is the sky blue?
fields.short_answer: Sunlight contains many colors. Tiny molecules in the atmosphere scatter blue light strongly in every direction, so blue light reaches your eyes from across the sky.
fields.big_idea: The sky is not painted blue; the air redirects part of sunlight before it reaches you.
fields.try_it: Add one or two drops of milk to a clear glass of water and shine a flashlight through it from the side. Look at the beam from the side, not into the light.
fields.try_note: Ask an adult to help with the glass and wipe up any spills.
fields.related_prompt: Explain why sunsets look red using the same idea that makes the sky blue.

fields.question: Where does a rainbow end?
fields.short_answer: A rainbow has no fixed end on the ground. It is light reaching your eyes at a particular angle, so when you move, the rainbow you see moves too.
fields.big_idea: Each observer sees a slightly different rainbow centered on their own viewpoint.
fields.try_it: After rain, stand with the Sun behind you and look toward the darker part of the sky. Notice how the bow stays opposite the Sun as you change position.
fields.try_note: Never look directly at the Sun.
fields.related_prompt: Why can two people standing apart see different rainbows?

fields.question: How do birds know where to go?
fields.short_answer: Migrating birds combine several clues. Depending on the species, they may use the Sun, stars, landmarks, smells, and signals from Earth’s magnetic field.
fields.big_idea: Navigation is not one built-in map. It is a toolkit that different birds use in different ways.
fields.try_it: From one quiet spot, watch birds for ten minutes and draw the direction each one travels. Repeat at another time of day and compare your map.
fields.try_note: Watch from a distance; do not chase, touch, or feed wild birds.
fields.related_prompt: Tell me about one bird that navigates by stars and how scientists tested it.

fields.question: Why do leaves change color?
fields.short_answer: As days shorten, many trees stop replacing green chlorophyll. Yellow and orange pigments become easier to see, and some leaves also make red pigments.
fields.big_idea: Autumn color is not one switch. It is the changing balance of several pigments inside a leaf.
fields.try_it: Collect only fallen leaves and arrange them from green to yellow, orange, red, and brown. Revisit the same tree a week later and compare.
fields.try_note: Leave living leaves on the tree and wash your hands after handling plants.
fields.related_prompt: Why do some trees turn red while others mostly turn yellow?

fields.question: Why can I hear the ocean in a shell?
fields.short_answer: The shell is not storing ocean sound. Its hollow shape emphasizes some of the ordinary sounds already around you, including room noise and sounds from your own body.
fields.big_idea: A shape can make certain frequencies louder by resonance.
fields.try_it: Compare a shell, an empty cup, and your curved hand beside your ear in a quiet room and then a noisier room. Listen for what changes.
fields.try_note: Hold objects beside your ear rather than pressing them tightly against it.
fields.related_prompt: What is resonance, and where else can I hear it at home?

fields.question: Why can I see my breath when it is cold?
fields.short_answer: Warm breath contains invisible water vapor. Cold air cools it quickly, so some vapor condenses into tiny droplets that scatter light and make a little cloud.
fields.big_idea: The cloud you see is condensed water droplets, not the water vapor itself.
fields.try_it: Breathe gently onto a cool mirror and watch a mist appear, then disappear as the droplets evaporate.
fields.try_note: Use an ordinary cool mirror, not frozen or heated glass.
fields.related_prompt: Why does the little cloud disappear again after I breathe out?

fields.question: How does a seed know which way is up?
fields.short_answer: A sprouting seed senses gravity. Roots usually grow with gravity, while shoots grow against it and later bend toward useful light.
fields.big_idea: Plants can change their growth direction in response to gravity and light without having a brain.
fields.try_it: Sprout a dry bean against a damp paper towel in a clear jar. Once a root appears, turn the jar sideways and sketch how the root changes direction.
fields.try_note: Keep the towel damp, not soaked; discard the experiment if mold appears and wash your hands afterward.
fields.related_prompt: How can a root sense gravity when it has no eyes or ears?

fields.question: Why is the sunset orange when the sky was blue all day?
fields.short_answer: At sunset, sunlight crosses far more air to reach you. Most of the blue is scattered away along that long path, so the light that gets through is mostly orange and red.
fields.big_idea: The same scattering that makes the day sky blue removes blue from light that has travelled a long way.
fields.try_it: Shine a flashlight through a clear glass of water with a few drops of milk stirred in. From the side the water looks faintly blue; looking at the light straight through the glass, it looks orange.
fields.try_note: Use a small torch, not a laser, and never look at the Sun itself.
fields.related_prompt: Compare noon and sunset light paths through the atmosphere with a simple drawing.

fields.question: How do bees find their way back to the hive?
fields.short_answer: Honeybees use the Sun as a compass, correcting for how it moves through the day, and they learn landmarks near the hive. They can even read the pattern of polarized light in patches of blue sky.
fields.big_idea: A moving Sun can still be a compass if you also keep track of time.
fields.try_it: Watch a flowering bush for ten minutes and note which direction the bees leave in. Check again an hour later and see whether the flight line stays the same.
fields.try_note: Keep a calm distance of a few steps and don't swat at bees.
fields.related_prompt: Explain the honeybee waggle dance and how it encodes direction.

fields.question: Do sunflowers really follow the Sun?
fields.short_answer: Young sunflowers do. Their stems grow a little faster on the east side during the day and on the west side at night, so the heads swing west and back again. Once they bloom, most stop and face east.
fields.big_idea: Plants can move by growing unevenly, and an internal clock helps time it.
fields.try_it: Put a pot of young bean or sunflower seedlings on a sunny windowsill and mark which way the tips lean in the morning and in the evening.
fields.related_prompt: Why would facing east help a mature sunflower attract bees?

fields.question: Why does my voice sound strange on a recording?
fields.short_answer: When you speak, you hear yourself through the air and through the bones of your head, which carry low sounds well. A recording only captures the air part, so it sounds thinner than the voice you are used to.
fields.big_idea: What you hear depends on the path the sound takes to your ears.
fields.try_it: Hum with your mouth closed, then plug your ears with your fingers and hum again. The hum gets louder because more of it reaches you through bone.
fields.related_prompt: How do bone-conduction headphones use this same idea?
